statement.p: Verify the Divergence Theorem for the vector field and region:

static.solution:
With z_0=6
Let \mathcal{S} be the surface of the cylinder and \mathcal{R} the region enclosed by \mathcal{S}.
We compute the two sides of the Divergence Theorem: \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \text{div} (\mathbf{F}) \,dV We first calculate the surface integral.
Step 1. Integral over the side of the cylinder.
The side of the cylinder is parametrized by \Phi (\theta ,z)=(\cos \theta , \sin \theta ,z),\quad 0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\quad 0\le z\le 6 \mathbf{n} = \left\lt \cos \theta , \sin \theta ,0 \right> Then, \mathbf{F} \left(\Phi (\theta ,z)\right)\cdot \mathbf{n} =\left\lt 6 \cos \theta ,6 z,2\sin \theta \right> \cdot \left\lt \cos \theta , \sin \theta ,0 \right>=6 \cos^2\theta +6 z \sin \theta We obtain the integral \iint_{\mathrm{side}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{6} \int_0^{2\pi } \left(6 \cos^2\theta +6 z \sin \theta \right) \,d\theta \,dz=36 \int_0^{2\pi } \cos^2\theta \,d\theta +\left(\int_0^{6} 6 z \,dz\right)\left(\int_0^{2\pi } \sin \theta \,d\theta \right)=36\cdot \left(\frac{\theta }{2}+\frac{\sin 2\theta }{4}\bigg|_0^{2\pi }\right)+0= 36\pi Step 2. Integral over the top of the cylinder.
The top of the cylinder is parametrized by \Phi(x,y)=(x,y,6) with parameter domain \mathcal{D}=\lbrace (x,y):\, x^2+ y^2\le 1\rbrace. The upward pointing normal is \mathbf{n} ={\mathbf{T} }_x \times {\mathbf{T} }_y = \left\lt 1,0,0 \right>\times \left\lt 0,1,0 \right> =\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j} =\mathbf{k} = \left\lt 0,0,1 \right> Also, \mathbf{F} \left(\Phi (x,y)\right)\cdot \mathbf{n} = \left\lt 6 x,36,2 y \right>\cdot \left\lt 0,0,1 \right>=2 y Hence, \iint_{\mathrm{top}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} =\iint_{\mathcal{D}} 2 y \,dA=0 The last integral is zero due to symmetry.
Step 3. Integral over the bottom of the cylinder.
We parametrize the bottom by \Phi (x,y)=(x,y,0),\quad (x,y)\in \mathcal{D} The downward pointing normal is \mathbf{n} = \left\lt 0,0,-1 \right>. Then \mathbf{F} \left(\Phi (x,y)\right)\cdot \mathbf{n} = \left\lt 6 x,0,2 y \right>\cdot \left\lt 0,0,-1 \right> =-2 y We obtain the following integral, which is zero due to symmetry: \iint_{\mathrm{bottom}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} =\iint_{\mathcal{D}} -2 y \,dA=0 Adding the integrals we get \iint_{\mathcal{S}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} =\iint_{\mathrm{side}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} +\iint_{\mathrm{top}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} +\iint_{\mathrm{bottom}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} =36\pi +0+0=36\pi \quad\mathbf{(1)} Step 4. Compare with integral of divergence.
\text{div} (\mathbf{F} ) = \text{div} \left\lt 6 x,6 z,2 y \right>=\frac{\partial }{\partial x}(6 x)+\frac{\partial }{\partial y}(6 z)+\frac{\partial }{\partial z}(2 y)=6 \iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \text{div} \left(\mathbf{F} \right) \,dV = \iiint_{\mathcal{R}} 6 \,dV=6\iiint_{\mathcal{R}} \,dV=6\, \mathrm{Vol} (\mathcal{R}) = 6\cdot \pi \cdot 6=36\pi\quad\mathbf{(2)} The equality of \mathbf{(1)} and \mathbf{(2)} verifies the Divergence Theorem.
